messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 34

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Loss of Control: Lack of control, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Meaning: go over and over why the event happened to me, Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things, Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arjun is a 53-year-old South Asian man who came to the United States from a region that experienced prolonged civil conflict, and it is that conflict — not the immigration itself — that has quietly dismantled the life he spent decades trying to build. He works as a painter, a trade he has practiced for over twenty years, and until recently it was the thing that most defined him: the physical competence of it, the reliable transformation of a surface, the satisfaction of a finished wall. He is married, and his wife describes him as a man who used to be present. He sought help, he said at intake, because he could no longer pretend the problem was manageable.

The event that anchors everything occurred several years ago, when Arjun was visiting family in his home country. A marketplace explosion — sudden, without warning — killed several people within meters of where he was standing. He was not physically injured, but the sensory world of that moment — the pressure wave moving through his chest, the acrid chemical smell of burning debris, the absolute collapse of any sense that he could protect himself or the people around him — imprinted itself in a way that has not released him. It is that specific loss of control, that moment when the world simply stopped obeying any logic he understood, that lives inside him still.

Back in the United States, the triggers found him before he understood what was happening. On a job site one morning, a contractor slammed a dumpster lid and Arjun dropped to a crouch before he had consciously registered the sound. His body had already decided. He described standing up afterward, hands trembling, certain that every worker on the site had seen him — and that what they saw confirmed something he was beginning to fear about himself: that he was no longer capable of being the man he had been. Ordinary sounds — a car backfiring, a nail gun, a door banging in the wind — now reliably catapult him into a state of full physiological alert, his body tense and scanning, heart elevated, unable to return to baseline for the better part of an hour. This hypervigilance is not merely uncomfortable; it is exhausting in a way that has begun to affect the quality of his work, his concentration, his ability to finish a room cleanly.

The smell of burning — encountered sometimes when clients have fireplaces, or when he passes a construction site with torched materials — carries him back with a completeness that is almost physical. He described the sensation of his body assuming the posture of that marketplace: crouched slightly, arms raised, as though the impact is still arriving. The memory itself feels so extreme, so outside the register of ordinary experience, that he sometimes finds it difficult to believe it belongs to him — and yet it also arrives with overwhelming grief, a grief that is not only for the people who died that day but for the version of himself that existed before it. He has come to believe that the world is genuinely dangerous in a way he simply failed to understand before, and that this knowledge, once acquired, cannot be undone. Nothing feels meaningful in the way it once did; the work that used to ground him now feels like motion without purpose.

These appraisals — that he is diminished, that the world is unsafe, that meaning has drained out of ordinary life — drive the strategies he has assembled to stay functional. He works long hours deliberately, filling every available hour with physical tasks, because stillness allows the memories to surface. He avoids any news coverage of conflict or bombings, knowing that even a headline photograph can trigger an afternoon of intrusion. He goes over and over in his mind why this happened to him specifically — a rumination that promises resolution and delivers none, but that he cannot stop, as though the right answer would somehow metabolize the grief. Yet the busyness, the avoidance, the rumination all circle back: the hypervigilance stays elevated, the body remains primed, and the next trigger — a smell, a sound, a moment of helplessness — finds him no less vulnerable than the last time. His wife has noticed that he flinches at sounds she cannot hear. He has noticed that she has stopped asking him how he is. What he is most afraid of, he said quietly at the end of the first session, is that this is simply who he is now.
